brand_naming_playbook.overview: Startups that win the naming game follow systematic, linguistically-grounded strategies — not gut instinct. This knowledge base encodes the full spectrum of modern naming methodologies, phonetic science, domain tactics, and evaluation frameworks into actionable rules and heuristics for an AI naming agent. It draws from professional naming agency processes (Lexicon Branding, Igor, Catchword), academic research on sound symbolism (Klink 2000, Yorkston and Menon 2004, Motoki et al. 2022), analysis of 4,000+ YC/Techstars startups, and dozens of founder case studies from 2020–2025. The landscape has shifted dramatically: 54% of accelerator-backed startups now use non-.com TLDs, .ai domains grew 375% from mid-2022 to late 2023, and single-word arbitrary names have become the aspirational gold standard for funded startups.

pattern.description: Explicitly states what the company does. Leaves zero ambiguity but is the weakest trademark category (USPTO "merely descriptive" rejections are common) and limits future pivots.
pattern.best_for: Trust-critical B2B where clarity beats creativity.

pattern.description: Fabricated words with no dictionary meaning. Earn the strongest trademark protection and total brand ownership, but require heavy marketing investment to build meaning. Must still be pronounceable and phonetically pleasing, ideally 2–3 syllables.
pattern.examples: Xerox (from Greek "xero" = dry), Kodak (pure invention), Hulu
pattern.best_for: Brands seeking maximum trademark protection and complete ownership.

pattern.description: Real words used figuratively. Create storytelling potential and earn "suggestive" trademark status (stronger than descriptive).
Signal large, established corporations. Research shows they work better after a brand is established — IBM was International Business Machines first.

Combine two recognizable words where both retain meaning, delivering immediate comprehension with distinctiveness. Per Arora et al. (2015), compounding accounts for 34.1% of top 500 global brands. Tip: combine an unexpected modifier with a familiar noun.
pattern.stat: 34.1% of top 500 global brands use compound names.
pattern.best_for: Brands wanting immediate comprehension with distinctiveness.

pattern.description: Merge parts of two words. Three blending methods exist: truncation (cutting parts off both words), overlapping (merging at shared phonemes), and fusion (combining without overlap). The blend must preserve the stressed syllable of each source word and result in 2–3 syllables.
pattern.examples: Pinterest (pin + interest), Instagram (instant + telegram), Netflix (internet + flicks), Groupon (group + coupon)
pattern.best_for: Brands wanting a distinctive coined name that hints at meaning.

pattern.description: No inherent product connection. Maximum brand flexibility and trademark strength, but maximum marketing investment required.

Apply common words to unrelated categories. Strong trademark protection, instant memorability, but premium single-word .com domains are scarce. Research shows names between 5–12 letters perform best for recall.
pattern.examples: Stripe (payments), Slack (communication), Linear (project management), Notion (productivity), Discord, Calm
pattern.best_for: Brands wanting memorability with trademark strength.

pattern.description: Account for 39.7% of top 500 global brands historically — the single largest category — but are declining in modern tech. Signal personal accountability.
pattern.best_for: Professional services, luxury, and craft brands.

pattern.description: Deliberately manipulate spelling. The "-r without e" pattern (Flickr, Tumblr, Grindr) is well-established. Emerged partly from domain scarcity. Caution: the name must pass the "phone test" — people must intuit the correct spelling.
pattern.best_for: Brands where a slight spelling twist adds distinctiveness without confusion.

pattern.description: Borrow from non-English languages. French/Italian words convey luxury; Japanese conveys precision; Latin conveys authority.
pattern.best_for: Brands wanting cultural connotations from a specific language.

pattern.description: Carry built-in narrative. Best when there is authentic alignment between the archetype and brand values.
pattern.examples: Nike, Amazon, Palantir (Tolkien's seeing-stone), Oracle, Pandora
pattern.best_for: Brands with natural alignment to a mythological or historical archetype.

pattern.description: Associate with place qualities. Risk: limiting perception if the company outgrows the geography.

pattern.description: Use puns, alliteration, onomatopoeia. Highly memorable when well-executed but risk seeming unprofessional.
pattern.best_for: Consumer brands where memorability outweighs formality.

pattern.description: Add tech suffixes to root words. Data from 2,127 startups shows -er is the most popular suffix (89 startups), followed by -ly (37) and -it (26).
pattern.best_for: Brands wanting a coined feel anchored in a recognizable root.

pattern.description: Use first names as brand names. Especially effective for AI/chatbot products where trust and approachability matter.
pattern.examples: Alexa, Siri, Oscar (health insurance), Ada (customer service AI), Harvey (legal AI)
pattern.best_for: AI and chatbot products where trust and approachability matter.

case_study.story: Hired Lexicon Branding — the firm behind BlackBerry, Pentium, and Swiffer. Lexicon created "Vercel" by combining roots from "versatile," "accelerate," and "excel." The "V" was deliberate: described as "the most alive and daring sound in the English language." The rebrand coincided with a $21M Series A; investors had struggled to take "Zeit" seriously.
case_study.lesson: Rebrands can signal maturity to investors, even when the community loves the existing name.

case_study.story: The Collison brothers thought "we could have this awesome mascot" (PayDemon). They also loved "PayForge" for its blacksmith/creation imagery. But the owner of stripe.com emailed back a reasonable price. Unable to decide, they set a deadline: if they couldn't find a better name by December 20, 2010, they'd default to Stripe — mirroring Apple's naming process. The name references the magnetic stripe on credit cards.
case_study.lesson: Setting a deadline forces decisions, and simple beats clever.

case_study.story: Founder Paul Copplestone wanted "ultrabase" or "hyperbase" — anything with "base." Everything was taken. "As a joke, I just put SUPA base and it was a placeholder." It stuck because co-founder Ant Wilson's favorite Nicki Minaj song is "Super Bass," enabling endless memes. After hitting the top of Hacker News, "we realized we can't actually change the name, so you're locked in." The unique spelling "supa" provided an unexpected advantage: Copplestone could track every single mention online because no other entity uses the word.
case_study.lesson: Memeability and uniqueness for social tracking are underappreciated naming advantages.

Applied the rename only to the parent company while keeping product names intact. Despite initial mockery, the rebrand succeeded: people now say "Meta," the stock recovered dramatically, and the company gained strategic direction. Cost: over $10 billion invested in Reality Labs.
case_study.lesson: Rename the parent entity while preserving established product names.

case_study.story: Destroyed 17 years of cultural equity — "tweet" and "retweet" had entered the English language. A Forrester poll found 43% called it a mistake; YouGov found 67% negative reactions. The letter X is one of the most commonly trademarked letters, making legal protection difficult. The @x handle was already taken on the platform itself. Users refused to adopt "posts" over "tweets."
case_study.lesson: No product transformation accompanied the name change. "It's one thing to rebrand if you're launching a completely new product. It's quite another to just slap a new name on an old product."

trend.description: Abstract names remain popular and are "increasingly getting popular with startup founders" because they allow brands to evolve. But there's a parallel trend toward semi-descriptive names that hint at function. The AI sector partly bucks this: many AI companies use highly descriptive names to establish legitimacy in a nascent field.
trend.insight: Startups initially opt for descriptive names to establish legitimacy; as industries mature, entrepreneurs shift to abstract identifiers.

trend.description: AI tools are widely used for brainstorming but experts note entrepreneurs are preferring human-generated names over AI-generated ones. AI-generated names often "simply combine two words with no thought behind them."
trend.best_practice: Use AI for volume ideation and expansion, human judgment for final selection.

trend.description: Mobile-first and voice search are driving shorter, more phonetically clear names. Voice-optimized domains — names easy to say to Siri, Alexa, or Google Assistant — are a growing 2025 priority.

pipeline.step: Map desired brand attributes to phoneme families using the sound symbolism tables.
Select morphemes carrying relevant semantic meaning from the 8,000+ English morpheme inventory.
Construct candidates using CVCV or CVC patterns with appropriate phonemes, targeting 4–8 characters and 1–3 syllables.
Apply hard filters: the radio test, trademark spectrum check (aim for fanciful or arbitrary), cultural screening across 10+ languages, and domain/handle availability.
Flag candidates scoring 70+ for professional trademark clearance.

heuristics.key_finding: The most counterintuitive finding across all the research is that naming constraints actually improve outcomes. Domain scarcity forces creativity. Trademark requirements push toward distinctiveness. The best names — Stripe, Notion, Linear, Figma — are not the result of unlimited brainstorming but of disciplined filtering.
heuristics.actionable_heuristic: Set a constraint, generate volume, filter ruthlessly, and commit. The Collison brothers' deadline trick (if we don't find something better by December 20, we default to Stripe) may be the most actionable heuristic of all.
